section.title: The Drought and the Prophet's Laments
section.sectionRationale: A devastating drought exposes Judah's helplessness even as false prophets promise peace, and God tells Jeremiah not to pray for a people so given over to judgment that not even Moses or Samuel could turn it back. In the middle of this darkness, Jeremiah confesses that God's words were his joy and delight, and receives a promise to be made a fortified wall against his opponents.
section.thesis: When drought and sword and famine come as covenant judgment, false prophets' promises of peace prove empty, and God's refusal to hear intercession shows how far Judah's sin has gone, yet even here Jeremiah's own confession, that God's words were eaten as joy, becomes the pattern for enduring faithfully under God's discipline while trusting His promise to sustain His messenger.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the drought that exposes Judah's helplessness and its people's confession of guilt; God's refusal to hear prayer for this people and His exposure of the false prophets promising peace; a second, more desperate cycle of lament asking whether God has utterly rejected Judah; God's severe reply that not even Moses or Samuel could turn back this judgment, rooted in the sins of Manasseh; and Jeremiah's own confession that God's words were his joy, met with God's promise to make him an unbreakable wall.

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the {{batstsoreth|drought}}:
“Judah mourns and her gates languish. Her people wail for the land, and a cry goes up from Jerusalem.

The nobles send their servants for water; they go to the cisterns, but find no water; 
their jars return empty. They are ashamed and humiliated; they cover their heads.
The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen on the land. The farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads.
Even the doe in the field deserts her newborn fawn because there is no grass.

Wild donkeys stand on barren heights; they pant for air like jackals; 
their eyes fail for lack of pasture.”
Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name. Indeed, our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You.
O {{tiqvah|Hope}} of Israel, its Savior in times of distress, why are You like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who stays but a night?

Why are You like a man taken by surprise, like a warrior powerless to save? Yet You are among us, O LORD, and we are called by Your name. 
Do not forsake us!

units.label: Do not pray for this people

verses.text:
This is what the LORD says about this people: 
“Truly they love to wander; they have not restrained their feet. So the LORD does not accept them; He will now remember their guilt 
and call their sins to account.”
Then the LORD said to me, “Do not pray for the well-being of this people.

Although they may fast, I will not listen to their cry; although they may offer burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them. Instead, I will finish them off by sword and famine and plague.”
“Ah, Lord GOD!” I replied, “Look, the prophets are telling them, ‘You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place.’”

“The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,” replied the LORD. “I did not send them or appoint them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a false vision, a worthless divination, the futility and delusion of their own minds.

Therefore this is what the LORD says about the prophets who prophesy in My name: I did not send them, yet they say, ‘No sword or famine will touch this land.’ 
By sword and famine these very prophets will meet their end!

And the people to whom they prophesy will be thrown into the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword. There will be no one to bury them or their wives, their sons or their daughters. I will pour out their own evil upon them.

You are to speak this word to them: 
‘My eyes overflow with tears; day and night they do not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people has been shattered by a crushing blow, 
a severely grievous wound.
If I go out to the country, I see those slain by the sword; if I enter the city, I see those ravaged by famine! For both prophet and priest travel to a land they do not know.’”

Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion? Why have You stricken us so that we are beyond healing? We hoped for peace, but no good has come, and for the time of healing, but there was only terror.

We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers; 
indeed, we have sinned against You.
For the sake of Your name do not despise us; do not disgrace Your glorious throne. Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it.

Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? Is this not by You, O LORD our God? So we put our hope in You, 
for You have done all these things.

units.label: Even Moses and Samuel
units.note: judgment rooted in the sins of Manasseh

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me: “Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people. Send them from My presence, and let them go.

If they ask you, ‘Where shall we go?’ you are to tell them that this is what the LORD says: 
‘Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.’
I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to drag away, and the birds of the air and beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.
I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem.
Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Who will mourn for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare?

You have forsaken Me, declares the LORD. You have turned your back. So I will stretch out My hand against you and I will destroy you; 
I am weary of showing compassion.
I will scatter them with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land. I will bereave and destroy My people who have not turned from their ways.
I will make their widows more numerous than the sand of the sea. I will bring a destroyer at noon against the mothers of young men. I will suddenly bring upon them anguish and dismay.

The mother of seven will grow faint; she will breathe her last breath. Her sun will set while it is still day; she will be disgraced and humiliated. And the rest I will put to the sword in the presence of their enemies,” declares the LORD.

units.label: Your words were found, and I ate them

verses.text: Woe to me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife and conflict in all the land. I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me.

The LORD said: 
“Surely I will deliver you for a good purpose; surely I will intercede with your enemy in your time of trouble, in your time of distress.
Can anyone smash iron, iron from the north, or bronze?
Your wealth and your treasures I will give up as plunder, without charge for all your sins within all your borders.
Then I will enslave you to your enemies in a land you do not know, for My anger will kindle a fire that will burn against you.”

You understand, O LORD; remember me and attend to me. Avenge me against my persecutors. In Your patience, do not take me away. 
Know that I endure reproach for Your honor.

Your words were found, and I {{akal|ate}} them. Your words became my joy 
and my heart’s delight. For I bear Your name, O LORD God of Hosts.
I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them. Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone, for You have filled me with indignation.

Why is my pain unending, and my wound incurable, 
refusing to be healed? You have indeed become like a mirage to me, water that is not there.

Therefore this is what the LORD says: 
“If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence. And if you speak words that are noble instead of worthless, you will be My spokesman. It is they who must turn to you, but you must not turn to them.
Then I will make you a {{chomah|wall}} to this people, a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you but will not overcome you, for I am with you to save and deliver you, declares the LORD.
I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless.”

batstsoreth.gloss: Drought, a withholding of rain. Deuteronomy 28 names drought among the covenant curses for disobedience, so this natural disaster carries theological weight, a visible sign that the covenant relationship has been broken.

tiqvah.gloss: Hope, expectation. Jeremiah addresses God directly as the Hope of Israel even while lamenting His apparent silence, modeling faith that keeps calling on God by His true character even in the middle of unanswered longing.

akal.gloss: To eat, consume, or devour. Jeremiah describes finding and eating God's words as joy and delight, an image of Scripture becoming genuine nourishment, later echoed when Ezekiel is told to eat a scroll, Ezekiel 3:1-3.

chomah.gloss: A wall, especially a city's defensive wall. God promises to make Jeremiah a fortified wall of bronze against his opponents, an image of unbreakable protection that anticipates Christ's promise that the gates of hell will not prevail against His church.

basic.context: A severe drought strikes Judah, cisterns run dry, animals are abandoned, and even the ground cracks open. The people cry out, confessing their guilt, yet God tells Jeremiah not to intercede, exposing that false prophets have been promising peace and prosperity in His name without His sending them. A second wave of lament asks whether God has utterly rejected Judah, and God's answer is severe: not even Moses or Samuel, Israel's greatest intercessors, could turn back this judgment, decreed because of what Manasseh did generations before. In the middle of this darkness, Jeremiah confesses that God's words were found and eaten as joy, and receives God's own promise to make him an unbreakable wall against his opponents.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage combines communal lament liturgy, divine refusal, and personal confession in a way that models honest faith under judgment: the people's prayer sounds pious, yet God exposes that repentance detached from a changed life cannot avert consequences already set in motion. Jeremiah's own confession in 15:10-18 is startlingly raw, bordering on accusing God of becoming like a mirage, yet God does not rebuke this honesty; He answers it with a call to return and a promise of strength.
basic.originalLanguages: The batstsoreth, drought, becomes the occasion for exposing both false prophets and Judah's own hollow repentance. Jeremiah calls God the tiqvah, Hope, of Israel even while lamenting His apparent absence. Later Jeremiah confesses that he akal, ate, God's words as joy and delight, an image of internalizing revelation as nourishment. And God promises to make him a chomah, wall, of bronze that cannot be overcome.
basic.typology: Jeremiah eating God's words as joy and delight anticipates the pattern later commanded of Ezekiel, who is told to eat a scroll, Ezekiel 3:1-3, and ultimately points to Christ, the living Word, whom believers are nourished by, John 6:35. God's promise to make Jeremiah an unbreakable wall anticipates Christ's promise that the gates of hell will not prevail against His church, Matthew 16:18.
basic.christ: Jeremiah's confession, Your words were found, and I ate them, and they became my joy, anticipates Jesus' own words, man shall not live on bread alone but on every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, Matthew 4:4, and finds its fullest expression in Christ, the Word made flesh, who is Himself the bread of life, John 6:35. And where God tells Jeremiah not even Moses or Samuel could intercede successfully for this generation, the gospel reveals a greater intercessor still, Christ, whose intercession never fails, Hebrews 7:25.
basic.god: God is willing to hear honest lament, yet He will not accept repentance detached from a changed life, and He exposes false prophets speaking comfortable lies in His name without His sending them. His refusal to hear intercession even from figures as great as Moses and Samuel reveals the severity of accumulated, generational sin, yet His personal answer to Jeremiah, offering renewed strength and protection, shows His discipline is never separated from His care for those who remain faithful to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 32:11-14 shows Moses interceding successfully for Israel, one of the two great intercessors named here. Ezekiel 3:1-3 pictures a prophet eating a scroll, echoing Jeremiah's image. Matthew 4:4 has Jesus quote the principle that man lives by every word from God's mouth. Hebrews 7:25 promises that Christ's intercession, unlike any merely human intercessor, never fails.
basic.oneStory: This is the sober reality that a people can sin themselves past the point where even the greatest intercessors could turn back the consequences, and yet within that same darkness, God nourishes His faithful servant with His own words as joy and promises him unbreakable strength, patterns fulfilled in Christ, the true Word who feeds His people and the greater Intercessor whose prayers for His own never fail.

context.literary:
Chapters 14 and 15 are built as two rounds of lament and refusal, followed by a personal turn. The first round runs from 14:1 to 14:18: a poem on the drought (verses 2 to 6), the people's prayer (verses 7 to 9), the LORD's verdict (verse 10), the ban on intercession (verses 11 and 12), and Jeremiah's protest about the prophets of peace (verses 13 to 16), ending in his own tears (verses 17 and 18). The second round runs from 14:19 to 15:9: another communal prayer (14:19 to 22), another refusal that raises the stakes to Moses and Samuel (15:1 to 4), and a dirge in which God asks who will pity Jerusalem (15:5 to 9). Only then does the prophet speak for himself, 15:10 to 21.

The voices change without warning. Verses 2 to 6 are the LORD's word to Jeremiah, yet they read like the prophet's own lament; verses 7 to 9 are the people's, though no one introduces them; verse 17 returns to a weeping voice that could belong to God or to His messenger. The blur is deliberate. It shows a prophet standing between two parties and feeling both.

The drought poem descends a ladder: nobles in the city, farmers on the land, a doe in the field, wild donkeys on bare heights. Verses 3 and 4 close with the same line, 'they cover their heads', so shame is the refrain. Notice too that the people's prayer of 14:7 to 9 and 14:19 to 22 is never answered with a yes. Each is met with a flat verdict, and the second refusal is the harsher, because it does not merely decline to listen, it names the two greatest intercessors in Israel's memory and sets them aside.
context.historical:
Judah lived on winter rain. There was no great river to fall back on, so water was stored in cisterns, and when the rains failed the nobles of verse 3 were reduced to sending servants to dry holes. Deuteronomy 28:23 and 24 had warned that disobedience would turn the sky to bronze and the rain to dust, and Solomon's dedication prayer anticipated this very crisis, a land with no rain because the people had sinned, and a people who then confess and turn, 1 Kings 8:35 and 36. The prayer of 14:7 to 9 and 19 to 22 uses the vocabulary Solomon provided. What it lacks is the turning.

The chapters are not dated. Many place them after the death of Josiah, in the years of Jehoiakim, 609 to 598 BC, when the reform had faded and the Babylonian threat was growing, though the text itself gives no year. What it does give is a date for the guilt: Manasseh, who reigned fifty-five years, 2 Kings 21:1, and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, 2 Kings 21:16. Josiah's reform could not undo it, 2 Kings 23:26 and 27.

The prophets of 14:13 spoke in the LORD's name, so to ordinary hearers they sounded no different from Jeremiah, and their message of shalom was what a frightened city wanted. Psalm 99:6 lists Moses and Samuel among those who called on the LORD and were answered, so when God says even they would not move Him, the first hearers heard the strongest refusal their tradition could voice.
context.canonical:
The ban on intercession is one of the book's fixed refrains. Jeremiah is told not to pray for this people in 7:16 and 11:14, and the command comes here at 14:11 and again, in its sharpest form, at 15:1. Ezekiel, writing among the exiles, repeats the thought with a different trio, Noah, Daniel and Job, who could deliver only themselves, Ezekiel 14:14. The pattern is that righteous people can save themselves but not a nation set on its way.

Jeremiah 15:10 to 21 is the second of the so-called confessions, the private complaints of the prophet that run through chapters 11 to 20 and sit close to the lament psalms. Verse 20 deliberately returns to the call: the fortified bronze walls and the promise 'I am with you to save and deliver' were first given in 1:18 and 19. God is not offering something new. He is reissuing the commission, with a condition attached.

The image of eating the word is taken up when Ezekiel is told to eat a scroll that was sweet as honey, Ezekiel 3:1 to 3, and when John eats the little scroll that is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach, Revelation 10:9 and 10, which is exactly Jeremiah's experience of joy that turns to solitude. In the New Testament, the confusion between false peace and true is met by Jesus, who weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, and who is Himself our peace, Ephesians 2:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The first readers of this section were people who had already prayed. Verses 7 to 9 and 19 to 22 are the kind of prayer a believing Judahite would be glad to have said, and the book keeps them in the text so that the reader cannot say the people never cried out. The author's point is that a prayer can be correct in every phrase and still be refused, because the phrases are not backed by turning. The LORD's answer in 14:10 names the problem in a single image: the people love to wander and have not restrained their feet. A lament that leaves the feet where they were is a liturgy, not repentance.

The author also wants the hearers to weigh the voices around them. Prophets saying 'lasting peace' were comforting and popular; Jeremiah is despised for the opposite word. By recording that God did not send the comforters, the book hands the community a test, and later it will state it outright, 28:9.

Finally, the author lets the reader see the cost to the messenger. Jeremiah sits alone, weeps, accuses God of being unreliable, and is neither silenced nor flattered. The reader is meant to learn that the one who carries a hard word may be the loneliest person in the land, and that God will answer him personally, even while He refuses the nation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The command not to pray is addressed to Jeremiah about one generation at one hour of the covenant's history. It describes God's settled verdict on Judah, not a rule for believers. Samuel's own conviction in 1 Samuel 12:23, that to stop praying for the people would be a sin, stands in the same Bible, and the New Testament urges prayer for everyone, 1 Timothy 2:1, even while 1 John 5:16 recognises that some cases are beyond the asking.

The drought is likewise a record, not a formula. Judah's famine is read as covenant judgment because God said so through His prophet. Jesus refuses to read every tragedy that way, Luke 13:1 to 5. Believers should not conclude that every dry season is a sentence, nor that a suffering person must have sinned.

Jeremiah's cry that God has become 'like a mirage' is a prayer reported, not a statement of doctrine to be copied. What the passage does commend is the pattern: say the raw thing to God, in God's presence, and then listen for His answer, which here includes a call to return.

debates.question: Why is Jeremiah forbidden to pray, and does this limit intercession now?

views.label: A judicial pause for this generation
views.case: The ban appears three times (7:16, 11:14, 14:11) and is sealed in 15:1 only after repeated warnings. Read with 1 Kings 8:35 and 36, God's promise to hear prayers of confession in a drought has a condition: turning. Where the turning is absent, intercession cannot reach what the covenant already decreed. This reading treats the ban as specific to Judah's last decades.

views.label: A rhetorical way of showing how grave the sin is
views.case: Others point out that Jeremiah goes on pleading, 18:20 says he stood before God to speak good for them, and the prohibition is a way of telling the prophet, and the readers, that there is nothing more to be done. The force of 15:1 is the comparison with Moses and Samuel, who had succeeded in Exodus 32 and 1 Samuel 7:9, not a new rule about prayer.

views.label: A pattern that warns but does not forbid prayer today
views.case: Many interpreters see a boundary that Scripture does draw, as in 1 John 5:16, but they refuse to turn it into a policy for Christians, since Paul prays for his own people who are hardened, Romans 10:1.

debates.bearing: The passage does not forbid the church to intercede. It shows that intercession is not a spell, and that God's mercy goes by way of repentance, which is why we pray for turning, not only for relief.

debates.question: Is Judah punished for Manasseh's sin or for its own?

views.label: Judah bears the guilt of the fathers
views.case: 15:4 says God will make them a horror 'because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did,' and the people themselves confess 'the guilt of our fathers,' 14:20. 2 Kings 23:26 says Josiah's reform did not turn away the anger kindled by Manasseh. The nation is one body across time.

views.label: Each generation is judged for its own deeds
views.case: Jeremiah 16:12 charges the present generation with doing more evil than their fathers, and 31:29 and 30 and Ezekiel 18:20 reject the idea that children simply pay for parents. Manasseh in 15:4 is the pattern and the beginning, not the whole cause; this generation has chosen to continue.

views.label: Both at once, since the nation is a continuing community
views.case: The Bible speaks of corporate solidarity, a people shaped by earlier choices, and of personal responsibility, a person who answers for his own. 2 Chronicles 33:12 and 13 shows that Manasseh himself humbled himself; the sin lived on in the people who had adopted it.

debates.bearing: The text refuses both a fatalism that says nothing can be done and an individualism that says history does not matter: the past gives the shape of the problem, and the present generation still has to turn.

study.originalLanguages:
The prophets' promise in 14:13 is 'lasting peace', literally shalom emet, peace of truth. The prophets are not offering mere quiet; they claim a peace that is reliable. Jeremiah's point in 14:14 is that the word behind it is sheqer, falsehood, and the verse then lists what they use instead of a message: a 'false vision', a 'worthless divination', 'the futility and delusion of their own minds.' Divination is the forbidden art of Deuteronomy 18:10, and the word for 'futility' is the one used elsewhere for idols, so the prophets' practice is described as a kind of paganism in the LORD's name. The pivot is 'I did not send them', where the verb is shalach, the very verb of Jeremiah's own commission, 1:7. Sending is what makes a prophet; they ran without it, 23:21.

The judgment in 14:12 uses a triad, cherev, ra'av, dever: sword, famine and plague. The same three recur through the book, for instance 21:9 and 38:2, and become a kind of shorthand for the siege that is coming.

In 15:6 the BSB says 'I am weary of showing compassion'. The verb behind 'showing compassion' is nicham, the word usually translated 'relent', as when the LORD relented in Exodus 32:14 and when He promises to relent if a nation turns, 18:8. The sentence therefore means that God is tired of relenting. A long history of reprieves is exhausted, and the shock is that the God who relents is the God who speaks here.

Verse 16 says 'Your words were found', then 'I bear Your name'. The Hebrew idiom is 'Your name is called over me', the same formula the people use in 14:9, 'we are called by Your name', as a plea. The people claim the name as a protection; Jeremiah, who bears it as a burden, truly lives under it.

In 15:18 the 'mirage' is akhzav, a word of disappointing deception, and the wound is 'anush, incurable, a root that Jeremiah uses of the heart in 17:9 and of the day of despair in 17:16, so his wound and Judah's heart share a word.

In 15:19 the call is a play on shuv: 'If you return, I will restore you', literally 'I will bring you back'. Then 'you will stand in My presence', using the verb of 15:1, amad, to stand before Me. Moses and Samuel stood before Him; Jeremiah is invited to stand where they stood. His task is to utter what is 'noble instead of worthless', the Hebrew yaqar against zolel, precious against vile, so that he becomes, in a literal rendering, 'like My mouth'.

typology.fulfillment: Moses stood in the breach and the LORD relented, Exodus 32:11 to 14; Samuel cried out and the LORD answered, 1 Samuel 7:9. They are the great types of the man who stands between God and a sinful people. Verse 1 declares that even they would fail here. The escalation is Christ, counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, Hebrews 3:3, who always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short because both men were sinners and mortal, and their prayers worked only inside the terms of a covenant people's repentance; Christ's intercession rests on His own offering.

typology.type: The prophet who eats the word, 15:16
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah finds the words and eats them, the sweetness a sign of true calling; Ezekiel is told to do the same, Ezekiel 3:1 to 3, and John, Revelation 10:9 and 10. In each case the word is sweet in the mouth and bitter in what follows. The pattern is fulfilled when the Word becomes flesh, John 1:14, and says that whoever comes to Him will never hunger, John 6:35. The type falls short because the prophet receives the word and delivers it; Christ is the word, and what He gives is Himself.

typology.type: The prophet who bears reproach for God's sake, 15:15
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah says he endures reproach for the LORD's honor. Psalm 69:7 to 9 gives the same sentence from the other side: scorn endured for God's sake, and insults falling on the righteous. Paul quotes the psalm of Christ, 'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me,' Romans 15:3. The correspondence is that the faithful servant takes on himself what is thrown at God. The escalation is that Christ bears it with no sin of His own, and no prayer for vengeance, Luke 23:34. Jeremiah's request in 15:15 shows how far even the best prophet falls short of that.

typology.type: The drought and the thirst for living water, 14:3 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The cisterns are empty and the jars come back dry. Later in the book God says that His people forsook Him, the fountain of living water, for broken cisterns, 2:13, and the image of an unfailing spring is taken up by Jesus, who says that if anyone thirsts he should come to Him and drink, John 7:37 and 38. The drought becomes a picture of a people cut off from the only source. The type is limited, since the drought in Judah is a judgment on a covenant nation, while the water Christ gives is a free gift, Isaiah 55:1 and Revelation 22:17.

study.christ:
Chapter 14 asks for a mediator who can do what Moses and Samuel could not, and the New Testament answers that He exists. The refusal of 15:1 is a statement about a people who will not turn, not about the limits of what a perfect mediator can do. Jesus is not another Moses standing in front of a hardening nation. He is the one who is both God and man, 1 Timothy 2:5, who offered up prayers with loud cries and tears and was heard because of His reverence, Hebrews 5:7, and who now has ground that no earlier intercessor had: He has borne the sin Himself. That is why the apostle can say that if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father, 1 John 2:1.

The weeping prophet of 14:17 is answered by the weeping Lord. Jeremiah's eyes overflow day and night for the city; Jesus, approaching Jerusalem, sees it and weeps, Luke 19:41, and in Luke 13:34 He gathers the same language of longing, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together.' In both the prophet's grief and the Lord's, the people are unwilling. Yet where Jeremiah is told to stop interceding, Jesus prays 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34.

The false peace of 14:13 is met by the real one. The prophets said 'peace' and there was none, as Jeremiah says in 6:14. Christ is Himself our peace, Ephesians 2:14, and the incurable wound of 15:18 and the 'beyond healing' of 14:19 meet the one by whose stripes we are healed, Isaiah 53:5 and Matthew 8:17.

Jeremiah's loneliness in 15:17, sitting alone because God's hand was on him, finds its deeper form in Gethsemane, where the Lord's soul is consumed with sorrow, Matthew 26:38. And the cry of 15:18, 'Why is my pain unending?', has its ultimate echo in 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46. The difference is that Jeremiah is invited to return, 15:19, because he spoke rashly, while Christ the sinless Servant is the one who is, in His desolation, still the Son who trusts. The promise of 15:20, 'I am with you to save and deliver you,' is made good in the resurrection and in His own word, 'I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20.

Caution is needed, though. Jeremiah is not Jesus, and not every feature of the drought is a picture of the cross. The links rest on the way the New Testament itself draws them: the mediator, the word eaten, the reproach borne.
study.god:
God is the one who governs rain. The people say as much in 14:22: idols cannot send showers, and the skies do not do so alone, so the God who withholds is the God who gives. The drought is therefore not an accident, nor a contest with a rival deity, but an act of the covenant LORD, who had told His people what would happen, Deuteronomy 28:23 and 24.

He is a God whose refusals are reasoned. The verdict of 14:10 does not say that God is capricious; it names the people's habit of wandering and their failure to restrain their feet. Fasting and offerings, 14:12, are refused because they are a substitute for turning, a point the prophets make again and again. When He says He is weary of relenting, 15:6, He is claiming a patience that has been tried, not a patience He never had.

God is truthful, and false speech in His name stirs Him particularly. In 14:14 and again in 14:15 He says He did not send the prophets, and 14:14 adds that He did not speak to them. His anger at lying prophets is not only about the harm to the people but about the misuse of His voice.

He holds together justice and mercy in a way that provokes questions. The same God who will not hear the nation's prayer opens His ear to the private grief of a single prophet and answers him personally, 15:19 to 21. The theology of divine relenting and divine constancy sits in the same book: God relents when a nation turns, 18:8, yet He is not a man that He should change His mind, 1 Samuel 15:29. The resolution is that His character does not change, so His response to turning and to refusal does not either.

He is faithful to His commission. The words to Jeremiah, 'I am with you to save and deliver you,' repeat what He said at the start, 1:8, so that His call outlasts the prophet's despair. The doubt of 15:18 is not met with a rebuke but with an invitation.

For worship this teaches us to bring our laments honestly and to expect an answer that heals the one who prays before it changes the circumstances. It also teaches us that a prayer is not a bargain: God hears the cry of the contrite, but He cannot be moved by words that leave the heart where it was.

crossReferences.note: The covenant curse in which the sky over Israel becomes bronze and the earth iron, and the rain is turned to dust and powder. The drought of Jeremiah 14 is the fulfilment of a warning that had stood in the law for centuries, which is why Jeremiah can call it covenant judgment and not merely misfortune.

Solomon's prayer asks God to hear when the skies are shut because of sin and the people pray toward the temple, confess His name and turn. Judah prays in the right form in Jeremiah 14:7 to 9, but the key condition, turning from sin, is missing, which is why the answer is 'no'.

Moses pleads with the LORD for a people who have made a golden calf, and 'the LORD relented from the calamity.' This is the pattern of effective intercession that Jeremiah 15:1 sets aside. The difference is not in the intercessor but in the situation: Exodus 32 is a single sin followed by grief, while Jeremiah faces a people whose turning never lasts.

Samuel tells a frightened people that he will not sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for them. This is the other half of the picture: an intercessor who refuses to stop. The pairing with Jeremiah 15:1 shows that the ban is about the situation, not about the value of prayer.

Even after Josiah's reform, the LORD did not turn from His burning anger, because of all that Manasseh had done. This is the historical note behind Jeremiah 15:4 and explains why even a godly king and a real revival could not clear the account.

The LORD says again that He did not send the prophets and that if they had stood in His council they would have turned the people back. It supplies the test that 14:14 implies: a true prophet's word moves people from their evil, a false prophet's soothes them in it.

The original promise to make Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls, with the assurance that his enemies will not prevail. Jeremiah 15:20 repeats it almost word for word, which shows that the prophet's despair in the middle of the book has not cancelled the call at the start.

A righteous sufferer bears scorn for God's sake and is a stranger to his own family because zeal for God's house consumes him. Jeremiah 15:15 and 17 describe the same experience, and Romans 15:3 applies this psalm to Christ, so the line from the prophet through the psalm to the Messiah is drawn by the New Testament itself.

Ezekiel is told to eat a scroll and finds it as sweet as honey. The picture is the same as Jeremiah 15:16, where words were found and eaten as joy. Both prophets show that God's word must be taken in before it can be given out.

Jesus is asked about those killed in a disaster and refuses to say they were worse sinners than others. It is a necessary check on reading Jeremiah 14: God had explicitly told Judah that drought would be His judgment, but we are not entitled to attach that meaning to every tragedy that happens.

In the days of His flesh Jesus offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears and was heard because of His reverence. Set beside the refusal of Jeremiah 14:11, it shows what kind of intercessor the nation lacked: one whose own obedience is the ground of the hearing.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a garden watered and a ground that gives; when Adam sins the ground is cursed, Genesis 3:17 to 19. Israel's land is a second garden given on conditions, and the drought of Jeremiah 14 is the old curse returning because the old pattern of disobedience has returned. In that sense the chapter answers a question left open since Eden: whether a people set in a good land can stay in it. By the time of Manasseh the answer is no, and Judah's history is heading to exile.

The chapter also continues the long search for a mediator. Moses stood in the breach, Samuel prayed, and now even they would not be enough. Each earlier intercessor delayed the judgment, and none removed the cause. The question therefore hangs: who can stand before God for a people who cannot turn themselves? The answer comes when the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy 2:5, gives Himself.

Meanwhile, God keeps His own promises through the dry years. The same book that records the refusal of 15:1 will soon say that the days are coming when God makes a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, and Ezekiel pictures 'showers of blessing,' Ezekiel 34:26. The rain that was withheld is promised again. Joel says the autumn rains will come as before, Joel 2:23. And the Spirit, the water that Isaiah 44:3 had promised, is poured out.

The thirst of 14:3 finds its final answer in Revelation, where those who come to the Lamb never hunger or thirst, and He leads them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:16 and 17. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1, and anyone who is thirsty may come and drink freely, Revelation 22:17. Even Jeremiah's own loneliness is answered: in the new creation God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3, and the prophet who sat alone is finally among them. The drought is not the end of the story; it is the sign of how far the story had to travel.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle, Part 3
sermon.why: Carson traces the two cycles of drought, prayer, and God's refusal across Jeremiah 14 to 15, along with Jeremiah's own prayers and God's response, exactly the movements this study covers.

quiz.q: What natural disaster forms the backdrop of Jeremiah 14?

options.text: A severe drought, leaving cisterns empty and the ground cracked.
options.note: Verses 1-6 describe this disaster in detail.

options.text: A great flood covering the land.
options.note: This is the opposite of the described drought.

options.text: A plague of locusts destroying the crops.
options.note: Locusts are not the specific disaster named in this passage.

options.text: A devastating earthquake striking Jerusalem.
options.note: Not the disaster described here; the chapter specifically concerns drought and lack of rain.

quiz.q: Why does God refuse to accept Judah's fasting and offerings in 14:12?

options.text: Because He will not accept them; He intends to finish the people off by sword, famine, and plague regardless.
options.note: Verse 12 states this directly.

options.text: Because God had already decided to bless the nation instead.
options.note: This directly contradicts the severe judgment announced in the verse.

options.text: Because the priests had stopped offering sacrifices altogether.
options.note: This contradicts the text, which describes fasting and offerings still being made.

options.text: Because the offerings were not the correct kind prescribed by the law.
options.note: The issue is not ritual correctness but a repentance detached from genuine change of life.

quiz.q: What does God say about the false prophets in 14:14-15?

options.text: He did not send them, and they will themselves perish by the very sword and famine they denied would come.
options.note: Verses 14-15 state this outcome directly.

options.text: They will be rewarded for comforting the people.
options.note: This contradicts the judgment pronounced on them in verse 15.

options.text: They were sent by God but exceeded their instructions.
options.note: God explicitly says He did not send them at all.

options.text: They spoke truthfully but were simply misunderstood.
options.note: God explicitly calls their message lies, false visions, and delusion, not truth that was misunderstood.

quiz.q: According to 15:1, why would even Moses or Samuel be unable to change the outcome?

options.text: Because God's heart would not go out to this people; He tells Jeremiah to send them away from His presence.
options.note: Verse 1 states this directly, naming Moses and Samuel specifically.

options.text: Because Judah had already been fully forgiven and needed no further intercession.
options.note: This directly contradicts the severe judgment announced in the passage.

options.text: Because Moses and Samuel had themselves sinned against God.
options.note: The text does not fault Moses or Samuel personally; it names them as history's greatest intercessors.

options.text: Because Moses and Samuel were no longer living and could not physically intervene.
options.note: The point concerns the severity of judgment, since the verse imagines them hypothetically standing before God regardless of their being alive.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah say about God's words in 15:16?

options.text: That he found them and ate them, and they became his joy and his heart's delight.
options.note: Verse 16 states this directly.

options.text: That he never actually received a word from God at all.
options.note: This contradicts the entire premise of Jeremiah's prophetic ministry and this very verse.

options.text: That he refused to receive them because of his suffering.
options.note: This contradicts his stated response of joy and delight.

options.text: That they brought him no comfort in his distress.
options.note: This contradicts the verse's description of God's words as joy and delight.

questions: The people's prayer in 14:7-9 sounds pious, yet God does not accept it as genuine repentance. What is the difference between saying the right words to God and actually turning back to Him?
The false prophets promised peace that was not coming. Where might you be tempted to believe comforting words over the harder truth God is actually saying to you?
God says not even Moses or Samuel could turn back this judgment. Have you ever faced consequences that prayer alone, however sincere, could not undo? How did you respond?
Jeremiah says God's words became his joy and his heart's delight even in the middle of suffering. What would it look like for you to find that same joy in Scripture this week?
God promises to make Jeremiah a fortified wall of bronze against his opponents. Where do you need to trust God's promised strength rather than your own ability to withstand pressure?

translationNotes.note: Drought appears among the covenant curses named in Deuteronomy 28:23-24, tying this natural disaster directly to the broken covenant theme running through these chapters.

Moses and Samuel were remembered as Israel's two greatest historical intercessors, Exodus 32:11-14 and 1 Samuel 7:8-9 and 12:19-23, making the statement that even they could not prevail here especially severe.
I bear Your name may allude to being formally called by God's own name, marking Jeremiah as one who belongs to the LORD in a way that carries responsibility as well as identity.
